title: Council Post: Cybersecurity Measures For Remote Hiring: Ensuring Confidentiality And Data Protection
text:
Chief Revenue Officer at Airswift.
Remote hiring is surging, reshaping how companies attract and onboard new talent. This shift brings convenience and broader talent pools but also ushers in heightened cybersecurity risks. Cybercriminals are increasingly targeting remote hiring processes, in which unsecured networks and the challenges of verifying identities online present unique threats.
These vulnerabilities can pose risks to the integrity of hiring procedures and have quantifiable impacts. According to IBM’s 2023 Cost of a Data Breach report, the global average data breach cost in 2023 was $4.45 million, a 15% increase over three years.
The urgency for robust cybersecurity in remote hiring is clear, and AI is proving to be a necessary ally. AI is revolutionizing cybersecurity by providing advanced tools for more effective risk detection and mitigation. Integrating AI with cybersecurity is essential to protect the remote hiring process, ensuring digital recruitment is both convenient and secure.
Secure Communication In Remote Hiring
Secure communication is crucial in remote hiring, as it involves sharing sensitive details like personal data, employment history and confidential corporate information. Safeguarding this data is essential throughout the digital hiring journey, from interviews to contract signings.
Encryption plays a key role here, with apps like Signal and WhatsApp providing end-to-end encryption to keep conversations private, transforming them into formats decipherable only by intended recipients.
Further enhancing security, AI can monitor communication patterns to spot anomalies such as potential data breaches or unauthorized access. By alerting IT teams to unusual data movements, AI, combined with encryption, forms a robust defense, preserving the integrity of the remote hiring process.
Safeguarding Sensitive Information With Data Encryption
Data encryption acts as a sophisticated lock, accessible only with the right key, ensuring that sensitive information is available solely to authorized individuals. It converts readable data into a coded format, rendering it indecipherable to unauthorized interceptors. In remote hiring, where personal, financial and confidential business data are regularly exchanged online, encryption is crucial to prevent data breaches that could lead to identity theft, financial loss or reputational damage.
AI-powered encryption solutions are vital in this context as they can adapt to changing threats. These systems continuously evolve, detecting new risks and fortifying data protection. For example, AI can identify unusual data access patterns and automatically tighten security, enhancing encryption against complex cyberattacks. This fusion of AI with encryption strategies elevates data security and improves the efficiency of safeguarding sensitive information in our digital era.
Protecting Data And Systems With Strict Access Controls
These include the personal information of candidates, internal HR systems and confidential company documents. Without stringent access controls, there's a heightened risk of sensitive information falling into the wrong hands.
Consider a scenario in which an HR system with loose access controls allows employees to view or edit confidential candidate data. This could easily lead to a data breach, where an unauthorized person accesses or leaks sensitive information, resulting in noncompliance with data protection regulations like GDPR or HIPAA. Such breaches expose individuals to risks like identity theft and subject the company to legal penalties, loss of trust and reputational damage.
Incorporating AI into access control systems significantly bolsters security. It monitors user activities, identifies irregular access patterns, enforces policies automatically and blocks unauthorized attempts to access sensitive information. This proactive approach is vital in maintaining the integrity of the hiring process and ensuring that only authorized personnel can access sensitive data.
How AI Helps Businesses Detect Threats And Prevent Cyberattacks
Remote hiring processes are increasingly targeted by cyber threats like phishing, malware and ransomware. Since the pandemic began, Deloitte reports a 25% rise in employees encountering fraudulent corporate emails.
AI systems can be trained to recognize patterns and anomalies that might elude human detection, such as subtle email address discrepancies or hidden malware within documents. An AI system can scan an email attachment and identify it as a potential threat based on its characteristics, even if it appears legitimate to a human reviewer.
This AI-driven approach to cybersecurity in the hiring process not only enhances the detection of threats but also speeds up the response time to potential breaches. By automating the analysis of communication and data exchanges, AI systems provide an additional layer of protection, ensuring that the hiring process remains secure and trustworthy in the face of evolving threats.
However, AI-driven cybersecurity has its challenges. High initial costs, complexity requiring user training and the possibility of false positives or negatives complicate their use. Continuous updates are essential to combat new threats, adding to maintenance demands. Compliance with evolving legal and regulatory standards also requires regular system reviews and adjustments. These factors suggest that AI cybersecurity, while beneficial, may not be the ideal solution for every organization.
AI And The Future Of Remote Hiring
The importance of cybersecurity in remote hiring cannot be overstated. Robust cybersecurity measures are essential throughout the hiring process, from handling sensitive candidate information to safeguarding internal communications.
Incorporating AI-driven solutions offers a significant advantage to an organization's hiring processes. AI's ability to examine patterns, detect irregularities and respond swiftly to potential threats ensures that only authorized individuals access sensitive data and helps quickly identify and mitigate cybersecurity risks.
Despite its challenges, advanced cybersecurity measures can protect against data breaches and ensure compliance, fostering trust with candidates and employees. In today's era of prevalent remote hiring, investing in AI-enhanced cybersecurity is essential but requires careful navigation of its complexities. It's not just a precaution but a strategic imperative for secure business operations.

title: Council Post: The AI Productivity Boom Is Here—Is Your Company Ready To Seize It?
text:
Brian Crotty, CEO, Fusion Connect.
The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution is underway—and in many cases, if your company didn't move yesterday, you could already be behind.
AI has seeped into every aspect of the workplace, and Gartner predicts that 90% of companies worldwide will be using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT by 2025. Why? Because they're leading to gains in productivity and efficiency that haven't been seen in our lifetimes.
According to Stanford and MIT researchers, generative AI boosted one tech company's productivity by 14%. That's 10 times more than McKinsey's recent estimate of a 1.4% growth in workplace productivity since 2005—a period that has included the widespread adoption of mobile devices and collaborative platforms.
How can that happen? AI tools are handling routine tasks so workers can focus on meeting broader, loftier goals that require human creativity. By exploring what these tools do and implementing them responsibly, you can unleash a new level of efficiency at your organization—but only if you act prudently and decisively.
Recognize the competitive advantage.
Your employees should use AI tools to make work easier, but you should assure them these tools won't displace them from their jobs.
AI can automate up to 70% of repetitive tasks, including document summarization, and text, image and code generation. Tools like Microsoft Copilot and Duet AI for Google Workspace can help recap email chains, put together a last-minute presentation or transcribe missed meetings. They free workers to spend their energy on value-added responsibilities such as managing client relationships and developing product strategies.
Our marketing team, for example, developed an AI-powered chatbot that has led to a 90% reduction in inquiries to team members for standard information. We've also built an AI tool that feeds contact information from scanned business cards directly into Salesforce.
For knowledge-based companies, AI can unlock faster data analysis, research and decision-making. For process-based organizations, it can spur continuous improvement in automation. This shift doesn't spell widespread job loss but rather a change in the nature of work that may lead to retraining and upgrading skills. As the Institute of Labor Economics found, most technology adopters have historically responded to labor shifts by expanding business and restructuring workflows to require more specialized workers—in this case, prompt engineers.
These gains in productivity translate to the bottom line. We're seeing a measurable impact in our customer service, where generative AI monitors client interactions to provide personalized outputs and significantly reduce response times. It automatically and instantaneously provides assistance that turns our front-line agents into experts, leading to a better customer experience, more satisfied customers and repeat business.
Spearhead AI's adoption.
AI is accelerating many aspects of work, but without oversight and proper application, its potential may be wasted.
Vague calls to your workforce to "go use AI" won't cut it. Lean into the technology yourself and provide regular examples of how AI will increase performance across departments. Dig into what these tools offer and determine how you can leverage them to achieve an ideal outcome. Put clear guardrails and guidelines in place that govern privacy, security and accountability so your teams understand boundaries. Develop best practices that prioritize use cases, and standardize how you approach tasks.
Foster collaborative pods for sharing AI techniques and use cases. That way, you'll build a sense of community, surface possible issues and develop checks and balances. You'll also reduce some of AI's more prominent risks, like a tendency to make up, or "hallucinate," information. A recent survey on AI adaptation in the workplace showed that while 56% of respondents said the models' inaccuracy is their top concern, only 32% say they're mitigating it. By doing so, you're already taking steps toward optimizing AI's use.
Of course, there are other risks to consider, including biases that emerge from training data, questions over intellectual property and fair use, and a possibility of automating or scaling mistakes. Don't be afraid to course-correct when something changes. These tools evolve quickly. What works for your organization today may be counterproductive tomorrow.
If you're invested in leading this change, you'll demonstrate how harnessing AI's power is paying off in the short and long terms.
Train an AI-ready workforce.
AI may hold tremendous potential, but you must always remember your people are your most valuable asset. Like with any other innovation, if you're not properly training your employees on how to use it, you're not positioning anyone for success.
Give your teams time to explore the tools that promise to move their responsibilities forward. (Avoid letting them have free rein to open any platform, though; data analysts don't need to dabble in image generation.) Develop and hold training sessions that show what AI can and can't do for them. Rely on those collaborative pods you've set up to identify other AI vanguards across the company and let their insight shine through.
You must also remember that AI can be confusing for many—especially amid concerns of job displacement. Trepidation and reluctance are the biggest obstacles to its widespread use. But an AI-ready workforce understands when to lead with human intelligence, when to lean on AI tools and how to maximize both.
If you give your people the knowledge they need to collaborate with AI and not compete against it, they'll feel valued during an unsettling time in the workplace.
Separate yourself from the pack.
Few technological developments have offered as much of a first-mover advantage as what we're seeing play out with AI.
Many businesses still see AI as a buzzword. They have yet to try to work with it or take time to comprehend what it will do for them. By being proactive, understanding how AI tools work, and implementing them throughout your organization, you're already at the forefront of a new era of productivity.
The companies embracing AI today are gaining a drastic competitive edge. Those that don't are squandering their opportunities and watching rivals surge ahead in the market.
It's your choice: Lead the AI revolution or wonder what might have been.

title: Council Post: The AI Revolution Will Be Monetized Through Consumption Pricing
text:
Deon Nicholas is CEO and cofounder of Forethought.
There will be billion-dollar businesses built on AI—that much is clear. Generative AI, autonomous agents and other related innovations will transform companies and fuel the rise of a new generation of GAI-native unicorns. However, how will these fortunes be made? What's the most appropriate way for the value of AI to be monetized from the perspective of both vendors and customers?
AI is more than just a technological shift. Like the cloud before it, AI represents an entirely new way of thinking about the way software is built and consumed. As in the cloud era, the software industry will now adapt accordingly—evolving new approaches to pricing, packaging and business models. This is going to be an adjustment for technology providers and customers alike, and we need to start thinking clearly about its implications.
AI Shifts The Unit Of Value From Users To Jobs
This isn't the first time a disruptive technology has forced new thinking in business models. With the rise of cloud and SaaS, subscription pricing models emerged as a way to capture the value of on-demand deployment and rapid, continuous updates. For customers, this allowed far greater flexibility in consumption while better reflecting the way software is used, seat by seat. For vendors, subscriptions offered perpetually recurring revenue rather than the one-off sales of perpetual site-wide licenses.
In a pre-AI time, individual seat licenses made sense. The more people you have using the product, the more value you're receiving. However, how does this apply to an AI-powered tool whose value resides in getting more work done with fewer users? Simple: It doesn't.
There's a fundamental difference in the way software is deployed with or without AI. Without AI, you're empowering a user to perform a role—whether as a customer service rep, a purchasing manager or an HR staffer. With AI, you're focusing on jobs, not people—deploying AI to autonomously resolve support tickets, generate purchase orders or manage employee onboarding processes.
With that, the unit of value becomes more analogous to a human worker than a subscription service. How much would it cost you in terms of hourly labor to resolve this support ticket, order these laptops or schedule this candidate's interviews?
This isn't to say that an AI agent should pull the same kind of salary as a human being; that would defeat the purpose. Instead, this comparison provides a benchmark. At the high end, an AI agent should represent significant savings over an employee or consultant. At the low end, the vendor needs to cover the cost of providing the service (an amount that will decline rapidly in accordance with Moore's law) with a decent margin for profitability. Anything in between is fair game.
Price Points And Pricing Models For AI-Powered Solutions
Drilling down a level, many companies already have an idea of what it costs them to handle various types of support tickets, for example. If an agent who makes $16 an hour can resolve a level 1 ticket in about 15 minutes, that's $4. A level 2 ticket goes to a higher-paid agent and might take a little longer. Level 3 involves another jump in cost.
If an AI agent can handle these tickets with zero staff time, that's $4 you're saving for each level 1 ticket and correspondingly more for higher level tickets. If you're paying $1 per ticket for that AI agent, you're coming out way ahead. If the vendor spends 30 cents on compute to get it done, so are they. As with the cloud, it's a win-win for both sides.
As this suggests, we'll likely also see different price points for AI agents with different capabilities or specializations. The rate for a customer support AI agent might escalate in tandem with defined ticket types. A simple scheduling agent might come at a much lower cost than one, creating complex data visualizations and reports. As with human workers, companies will pay more for higher levels of expertise and value.
Once the core consumption model for AI has become more clearly defined and understood, packaging models like bundling can come into play. A company that knows it'll have at least 10,000 support inquiries per month could prepay at a discount for this volume and then true up for any overage at the usual rate. Conversely, companies focused on predictability could pay a premium for an all-you-can-eat rate at a high enough volume to cover their likely consumption.
In the spirit of everything-old-is-new-again, the Rolling Four-Hour Average (R4HA) used in the mainframe world offers a convenient model for calculating value based on system utilization, along with well-established optimization techniques for keeping costs down.
Navigating The Evolution To AI-Era Business Models
For AI-native companies, building consumption pricing into your business model is a relatively straightforward matter. For incumbent SaaS vendors, it's not quite so simple. When your whole operating model is based on seat pricing, from your P/L to the way your salespeople think, jumping to an entirely different approach is a daunting prospect. That's true, given the need to cannibalize your current annual recurring revenue.
Given this reluctance, it's understandable that some SaaS companies have launched new AI features with per-seat pricing, perhaps hoping to offset the reduction in user headcount by charging more for each. How well this approach holds up in a price-competitive market remains to be seen.
Value-oriented businesses will need to deploy the plumbing for this way of monetizing value, including billing customers, recognizing revenue and handling sales commissions. New businesses are already being created to provide metered or consumption pricing as a service.
The transformation to consumption pricing won't happen effortlessly, and not everyone will navigate it successfully. However, the gains will be well worth it. The cloud may have decimated the revenue model for on-premises software, but it also multiplied the total opportunity—providing a boost to the industry and the global economy.
AI will have a similar impact. Customers will pay less and get more, and service providers will capture the vast potential of this technology.

title: Council Post: Three Critical Steps To Implement Generative AI Safely, Economically And Effectively
text:
Debanjan Saha is CEO of DataRobot and a visionary technologist with leadership experience at top tech companies such as Google, AWS and IBM.
Generative AI brings tremendous promise in terms of opportunity, with an equal amount of challenges and risks when considering what could go wrong.
Now that organizations are waking up to the transformative power of AI, they are starting to search for ways to use it to increase efficiencies and improve product and service offerings to customers.
So far, much of this investigation has not led to actual implementation. That is because a confidence gap between generative AI accuracy and opportunity is holding many companies back, making them reluctant to move beyond planning.
Organizations that want to start taking advantage of generative AI and implementing real-world solutions need to take three steps to ensure safe, responsible, economical and effective deployment.
Step One: Protect Proprietary Data
Data is one of the most valuable assets within any organization, and concerns about data security have held many companies back from implementing generative AI.
There have been numerous examples of employees unintentionally feeding confidential data into publicly available generative chat experiences like ChatGPT, such as an employee who used it to find errors in a top-secret database.
Unfortunately, this made the classified corporate data part of ChatGPT's learning dataset. Once there, the data could be exposed to outsiders through a breach (such as the ChatGPT breaches reported in June 2023) or bad actors retrieving this confidential data by manipulating the LLM.
To protect their data, data and AI teams must make sure that no part of their internal data is exposed to these publicly available experiences. There are several types of foundation models to choose from (custom-built, private API calls or open source), and each one comes with its own set of trade-offs. Which LLMs are used, how they're hosted, what vector database and how it's built are key in protecting sensitive data. They also need to confirm that if an LLM is trained on or connected to sensitive data, outsiders can't access it.
Finally, data and AI teams must verify that all of the company's generative AI-related projects and users are visible to establish that no employees are going "off the grid" with risky projects.
Step Two: Provide Accurate Answers
The value of a generative AI solution is only as good as the quality of its output.
Many issues have been noted with generative AI solutions providing misleading or incorrect information. This can lead to wasted time and embarrassment in internal use cases.
In external use cases, the results can be even more damaging. If, for instance, a healthcare provider uses generative AI as a first line of customer support, incorrect or inappropriate answers can cost lives. The outputs could be dangerous even with lower-stakes applications, such as a recipe creation generative AI engine. In August 2023, just such an engine spit out creations that included hazardous ingredients.
With generative AI, there's an inherent risk of generating misleading or false information. Data and AI teams can help maintain the integrity of the results through the use of confidence scores with outputs that give users an understanding of how much confidence they should place in the answer from generative AI. Human feedback loops that allow users to qualify the answer as correct, incorrect or incomplete can also help teams monitor the quality of their generative AI solution.
Generative AI lineage and reporting should also be part of a generative AI strategy, where you can quickly pull reports and see which answers are wrong and what content the LLM used to create the answer it gave. Of course, using generative AI requires monitoring of toxicity or prompt attacks to help alert you if bad actors are trying to jailbreak your generative AI solutions.
Step Three: Don't Overbuild
With the potential that technologies like generative AI offer, it's easy for data and AI teams to get caught up in making massive changes that revolutionize every aspect of the company while overlooking smaller, discrete—but valuable—applications.
Data and AI teams should start by identifying specific challenges that could be streamlined using AI, prioritizing them and implementing them individually.
Trying to create a single AI solution that will work in multiple areas of the business will create more problems than solutions by increasing the risk of AI "hallucinations" and wrong answers as well as data security. It can also be a nightmare to maintain, govern and monitor.
Instead, leaders should embrace the idea of creating multiple applications that deliver immediate business value using generative AI, which can be easier to build, maintain and protect. Data and AI teams need to maintain flexibility for their foundation models and be able to hot-swap them out when new solutions become available that offer similar performance for lower costs.
It's also critical that those overseeing the technology receive alerts and have clear thresholds in place to be able to manage and monitor costs effectively.
Change in the generative AI space is occurring at a breakneck pace, and there is no clear standard or leader when it comes to generative AI components or solutions. Data and AI teams must have the flexibility to be able to mix and match the right offerings for the right tasks. Leaders can future-proof their tech stack and their generative AI solutions by retaining the ability to swap out specific elements (such as LLMs or vector databases) without disrupting production workflows and applications.
Moving Beyond Potential
Companies have woken up to the incredible, disruptive potential of generative AI. They now need to realize that potential. Doing so will require data and AI leaders to close the confidence gap with generative AI, minimize risks, have strong governance and observability policies and control costs while offering practical solutions.
In the meantime, AI leaders who win with this technology will be the ones who can identify the biggest individual opportunities across their organizations and can confidently and quickly move past prototyping to safe, accurate, cost-effective implementations in production.

title: Council Post: How To Embrace The Power Of AI: Four Patterns To Fuel Your AI Strategy
text:
Rajul Rana serves as the Chief Technology Officer at Orion Innovation.
Every decade or so, a technology comes along and disrupts everything around us. It changes the way we work, the way we play and the way we engage customers. In the '80s, the personal computer revolutionized our world, then the internet in the '90s, smartphones in the 2000s and cloud computing in the 2010s. Now, we are on the brink of another significant technological transformation driven by generative AI (GenAI).
AI has been around for decades. So, why is there a sudden buzz around GenAI?
This surge can be attributed to a confluence of factors coming together in the past two years. Advances in raw computing power, the exponential growth in available data, plummeting AI training costs and breakthroughs in machine learning algorithms, such as the transformer model, now deliver unparalleled sophistication. OpenAI was quick to harness these trends; they wrapped the technology in an approachable interface and created a killer app that started the revolution and has gained millions of users since its launch.
Foundational Models
GenAI is based on foundation models (FM) that allow it to understand context and relevance within the content it processes, making it incredibly powerful and versatile. The transformer architecture represents a paradigm shift in how AI processes text, offering unprecedented language understanding.
Building FMs involves two key stages: unsupervised training on vast amounts of content (text, images, etc.) and fine-tuning for specific tasks, such as Q&As. The process is complex and resource-intensive. Selecting what FM to use is the first step in building a GenAI solution.
Once you select an FM, you need to decide how you will build your GenAI application.
We have developed numerous GenAI use cases and have identified four solution patterns that enterprises can choose based on cost, complexity and accuracy.
Pattern 1: Out-Of-The-Box LLM API-Based Solutions
The most straightforward approach to generative AI involves leveraging readymade APIs from large language model (LLM) providers like OpenAI, Anthropic and others. This method is straightforward and doesn't require extensive development or data science skills. It simply requires building a front-end application that calls these LLM APIs.
User prompts are the primary mechanism to provide context in this approach. The better the prompt, the better the output. This has led to prompt engineering as a discipline in which prompt engineers can try different inputs to arrive at the “optimal” prompt that elicits the “best” answer.
While this pattern is quick to implement and requires minimal coding, accuracy is low as the LLMs have a limited "context window." A context window refers to the length of text an LLM can process and respond to for any given instance in a prompt.
This pattern is best for generic use cases that don’t require enterprise context.
Pattern 2: In-Context Learning
This popular pattern, also known as a RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) pattern, involves using cloud-based APIs from LLM providers while feeding them with enterprise context.
This pattern also leverages an API from the LLM provider, but there is a backend application that can take the enterprise content, break it down, vectorize it, store vectors in a database and, when a user query occurs, provide appropriate enterprise context through vector search as input to the model.
Unlike Pattern 1, the prompt engineering is done by the backend application, not by users. Pattern 2 balances simplicity and effectiveness, making it a go-to choice for many without finetuning existing models or building new ones from scratch.
This approach is a lot more accurate than Pattern 1 and can be built by regular application developers without machine learning expertise. However, this pattern has limitations due to the limited context window, particularly for domain-intensive use cases.
Pattern 3: Fine-Tuning Existing Models
An enterprise can fine-tune existing models with domain-specific content if it wants to go further with more accuracy and speed.
Fine-tuning is the process of adjusting model parameters. It involves training an existing open-source model on your labeled dataset, allowing it to change the model’s weights based on your data. Clean, curated datasets can speed up the training process and boost accuracy. This approach requires data science, machine learning expertise and meticulous data labeling of your content.
Based on our experience, we’ve found that it typically takes a few months to train an existing model on your domain-specific content. It's an iterative process and requires continuous evaluation and testing to ensure that accuracy is improving. If not, you need more relevant content or better labeling of content.
While this solution pattern is complex and expensive, it gives an organization a competitive advantage with higher accuracy and performance by tailoring models to specific tasks.
Pattern 4: Building Your Own Foundation Model
The most complex pattern involves building a custom model from scratch. It’s a significant investment and commitment but well worth it, especially if you have terabytes of unique data, and the GenAI use case can allow you to differentiate from and leapfrog over your competitors.
It requires vast data resources and advanced data science and infrastructure management expertise. While this option may seem out of reach for most companies today, as open-source tools emerge and GPU chips become more affordable, overall costs will come down, boosting the ROI for building models from scratch.
Selecting The Right Pattern
When choosing the appropriate pattern for your use case, consider the balance between cost, complexity and accuracy.
Most of our customers start with building proof of concepts using Pattern 2. Given its balance of effectiveness and feasibility, it’s no wonder that this pattern is the most popular. However, the field of GenAI is maturing rapidly, and I expect Pattern 3 (fine-tuning models) will gain prominence over time.
Each technological leap in the past 30 years has redefined our world. Fail to jump, and you're left behind. Choose one of the four solution patterns that align best with your company’s readiness, capabilities and goals. The key is to start experimenting, learning and continuously improving.

title: Executives Cautiously Hit The Brakes On Artificial Intelligence
text:
Close to three-quarters of executives, 72%, say they are purposely exercising restraint with generative AI investments, mainly due to societal pressures to use AI responsibly. However, as is the case with technology these days, if you don’t keep up, you could be out of business. So, they are cautiously exploring the potential of the technology — and corporate culture will be decisive in how it gets implemented.
These are among the conclusions drawn from the latest Accenture pulse survey on the state of business progress in 2024, drawn from a survey of 3,400 C-suite executives measured against key business indicators.
The executives surveyed agreed that “the recent backlash on generative AI — policy issues, lack of accuracy, low initial ROI — will cause our organization to slow down planned investment in gen AI in 2024,” the survey shows.
Emerging technology policies and regulations are also seen as a positive, as seen by 71% of the executives.
Organizational culture plays an important role in how AI is leveraged. In people-first cultures, leaders view AI as a tool, not something that should overtake their businesses. “It’s important that companies implement AI in ways that not only strengthen existing approaches, but also in ways that are ethical,” urges Keith Farley, senior vice president at Aflac.
Aflac’s view on AI is in line with its long-standing corporate culture, Farley continues. “We only employ AI in ways that ensure our customer’s best interests are protected. For example, we are comfortable with AI making simple claims approval decisions, but not complex ones. When it comes to making complicated assessments about an individual’s health plan and whether a health event is covered, a human always makes the final decision.”
The insurer’s products “touch people, sometimes during their darkest moments, and we will always need compassionate people to serve our customers in ways that machines cannot,” says Farley. “We have to remember that the first word in AI is artificial, and when you are going through a difficult time sometimes you want something authentic. We need to blend people and machine learning for the best, most authentic results.”
There is a lot of preparation work ahead. Only 27% of the C-suite executives in the Accenture survey say their organizations are ready to scale up generative AI, and 44% say it will take more than six months to do so.
Notably, however, 76% of the executives saw generative AI as more of an opportunity than a threat, and more beneficial to revenue growth than costs reduction.
This calls for business leaders stepping up to guide their companies’ AI directions. “Technologies like GPT are so accessible to everyone,” says David Higginson, executive vice president and chief innovation officer at Phoenix Children’s. “We strongly encourage all staff to use it in a safe and secure way and make their own determination of the value and opportunities for future use.”
Phoenix Children’s “chooses to focus on the adage ‘begin with the end in mind,” says Higginson. “For all our AI work, we always engage the end users throughout the organization and start the process by asking them, ‘if the AI solution we develop was 90% accurate in making a prediction, help us think through how you would use it in your workflows.’”
At least 48% of executives in the Accenture survey expect AI chatbots will have transformational change on their organization’s technology architecture over the next three years. At least 45% strongly agreed that AI agents will begin to collaborate with other agents to accomplish organizational tasks. At least 40% say their organizations are very prepared to integrate autonomous AI agents into their workflows.

title: Council Post: Boardroom Guide To Govern AI And Secure Its Adoption
text:
Steve Durbin is Chief Executive of Information Security Forum. He is a frequent speaker on the Board’s role in cybersecurity and technology.
Artificial intelligence and machine learning technologies have been around for decades. The arrival of ChatGPT threw this topic into the spotlight, generating widespread discussion and diverse opinions, especially regarding cybersecurity.
Now would be a good time for enterprises to get smart about AI security. This involves more than just protecting AI from cyberattacks or exfiltration of data—it is about protecting AI data from discrimination, bias, manipulation and privacy violations. Because it’s the data that fuels AI decisions.
Among mature organizations, it is the responsibility of board members and key executives to set direction on policies and processes for the secure adoption and long-term success of technologies like AI. But how do board members who are not particularly technology savvy create a secure foundation for such a rapidly evolving technology? Here are five practical considerations that can help:
1. View AI from the lens of corporate strategy and risk.
Board members might have difficulty understanding technology, but they can certainly understand strategy and risk. Before you can chart an AI strategy, develop a thorough understanding of its potential, its current usage across the organization and the security challenges and threats that lie ahead.
For example, what if the data or the algorithm becomes poisoned or is weaponized by hackers? Are current cybersecurity defenses adequate? What if the AI model starts miscalculating or misrepresenting data? Does the business have enough checks and balances in place to ensure confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and AI models? These are hard questions boardrooms should be asking.
2. Evaluate the impact of AI activity.
Now that board members have a better understanding of risks and opportunities, it’s important they consider the strategic implications of any AI products or services being used or under development. What is the true intention or end goal behind using AI? How will it impact existing processes? What is the business benefit that will be derived? How will AI impact employees, customers and stakeholders?
Let’s say AI assumes tasks or jobs originally performed by workers. Boards must understand cybersecurity implications. Are employees being trained in a manner that mitigates AI risks? Do employees feel empowered and in control? Boards may have limited knowledge of how AI interfaces with customers and the extent to which AI gathers information; it’s important they understand since this can have negative security and privacy implications.
3. Consider AI-related compliance and controls.
There’s a lot of opportunity surrounding AI; however, one shouldn’t underestimate the changing legal, regulatory, privacy and ethical landscape.
For instance, in the European Union, a new law being proposed (the EU AI Act) will require AI providers to ensure AI systems are designed and developed in a way that is "safe, transparent, traceable, non-discriminatory and environmentally friendly." Similarly, the Biden administration issued an executive order promoting the use of safe, secure and trustworthy AI. Regulations surrounding incident disclosure are also fast emerging.
As a result, organizations that develop AI-based technologies will come under increased scrutiny from regulators and lawmakers. This will in turn lead to greater demand for oversight from the board. It’s also entirely possible that boards will increasingly seek help from industry experts to help deal with matters concerning regulations and compliance.
4. Create a governance framework.
Working with security leadership, the board must create a governance framework that aligns with corporate strategy and addresses identified risks and compliance requirements.
I recommend that the board appoint an AI committee of cross-functional leaders such as the CEO, legal, HR, senior IT and security teams. This committee can oversee development of AI-related policies and procedures (best practices, guidance on use of generative AI, etc.) and accountability structures consisting of appropriate teams and individuals that can help maintain the accuracy and fairness in AI models and manage, measure and report AI risks.
5. Integrate ethical considerations.
Fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and security are some of the most pressing ethical issues surrounding AI today. To evaluate whether these ethical principles are being considered in the AI development life cycle, it is important that boards adopt practices such as appointing an ethics team that is both diverse and inclusive, conducting regular ethical risk assessments, implementing bias detection and introducing processes that ensures the AI system does not discriminate.
Organizations should consider informed consent; users must know that they are interacting with AI systems. Finally, there must be an element of human oversight that helps increase the safety and accuracy of AI systems.
AI is a rapidly evolving technology that will significantly expand the current threat surface. Keeping AI on the right track will require a sound governance framework, transparent and ethical policies, and adaptive security strategies, because regulations will not be standardized anytime soon. Boards have a central role to play, not just in the development of AI policies and processes, but in areas of cybersecurity. A robust security foundation is central to a successful AI rollout and long-term resilience.

title: Council Post: Why Higher Education Should Embrace AI Now To Advance Learning
text:
Elise Awwad is president and CEO of DeVry University.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and its related technologies are rapidly advancing and transforming industries across the globe. Higher education is no exception. An Educause poll shows a strong majority (83%) agree that "these technologies will profoundly change higher education in the next three to five years."
Like other industries, those of us in higher ed also seek to leverage AI’s capabilities to advance and enrich the value we deliver to stakeholders, such as building ways to remove barriers, eliminate friction, inspire and engage to ultimately drive lift in the return delivered.
The Google, Apple and Amazon effect has a halo effect on us all. Notably, consumers continue to be exposed to brands’ efforts to deliver intuitive solutions to them, which has resulted in tailored journey points across the consumer experience becoming a new norm. This raises the bar across industries to deliver on promises of personalization and quality—an expectation higher ed is equally subject to and cannot ignore. I think the best brands, and wise higher education institutions, will seize the moment to lead with AI and push outcomes to new levels.
AI and all it will bring will soon permeate our lives and workplaces, making it beneficial for students to gain exposure to and experience with these technologies. What better way to learn about AI in a controlled, supportive environment than in the classroom? While the effects of AI on education are still being studied, responsible and ethical use of it can serve to enrich and advance learning and empower institutions to deliver on students’ needs.
Here are several compelling considerations and reasons why colleges and universities should embrace AI sooner rather than later.
A holistic AI strategy is necessary.
Integrating AI into curriculums will produce graduates with in-demand skills to succeed in an AI-driven economy. This is one reason why higher education stands to lose more than it would from being an early adopter.
However, the integration of AI into higher education is an essential initial step that requires institutions develop comprehensive and strategic approaches. These approaches will serve as foundational roadmaps, guiding them in harnessing future opportunities and addressing emerging needs associated with AI.
Several educational institutions are at the forefront of technological innovation. For example, my organization launched an AI Lab to advance learner success. The lab spans all facets and functions of our institution as we seek to evolve our curriculums to reflect the urgent needs of the marketplace.
Allow AI to enhance learning by saving time and energy.
Further, educators today face immense challenges from managing administrative tasks to personalizing instruction for diverse learners. However, advancements in AI technology are helping to tackle these challenges and empower educators to focus on what matters most: student learning.
Higher educators can trade on the time and energy they invest in administrating education by leveraging AI and automation to make resources more accessible and streamline communication, thus, empowering them to spend less time on repetitive tasks and more time advancing learning in meaningful ways.
Empower personalized learning through AI for desired outcomes.
Learning is an inherently complex process and intricate journey. As we pursue new knowledge and skills, thousands of new connections are formed in our minds—and for each learner, that process differs. AI-based learning offers the potential to use adaptive platforms that can interpret these nuances and tailor the learning pathway to accelerate the learning process and lift outcomes.
For example, we’ve already witnessed the impact of AI in the classroom at DeVry. As early adopters of an adaptive learning technology designed to elevate outcomes in mathematics, we’ve seen learners who might otherwise face challenges, flourish when provided the right tools.
AI platforms can interpret and empower learners even as they tackle challenging topics, achieving a level of efficiency and scale that would be difficult to replicate in a traditional, faculty-only teaching model.
Prepare for the challenges.
When looking to introduce AI into the college and university eco-system, there are some challenges that administrators must consider ensuring a seamless implementation while avoiding unintended consequences.
One of the challenges is clearly thinking through ethical considerations, such as ensuring privacy and data security and mitigating biases in AI algorithms. Academic institutions must prioritize the establishment of ethical guidelines and emphasize transparency in AI applications, while also fostering an environment that encourages ethical discourse about the societal impacts of AI. It is important to ensure that AI technologies are inclusive and equitable, actively promoting diversity to prevent the reinforcement of societal biases.
Equally important is the focus on skill development and upskilling for both students and faculty to keep pace with AI advancements. This encompasses not just technical skills but also durable skills that are critical for navigating the AI landscape.
By proactively and thoughtfully addressing these challenges, colleges and universities can not only successfully integrate AI but also prepare their students for the future job market where AI will become a pivotal element.
Adapt, adopt or risk perishing.
The time for higher education to act is now. AI is here to stay, and higher education must keep up with the pace of change to remain relevant and continue fulfilling its purpose of educating and empowering learners.
There is no greater lesson than the importance of: adapt, adopt or perish. That mentality is needed to be at the forefront of skills development. AI offers the opportunity to harness the frontiers of innovation, and it requires higher education to lead the way in driving training, learning and development. This proactive approach is critical to prepare for and capitalize on the incredible opportunities ahead.

title: Council Post: A Stepping Stone Year For Generative AI: Core Challenges For 2024
text:
Naveen Zutshi is the CIO of Databricks.
In the year since generative artificial intelligence (AI) found its footing in broader public conversation, its application across enterprise technology has only grown—and so has enthusiasm among leaders.
The current period of innovation is just only beginning, and the work the technology industry is doing now will inform how AI will impact our lives and work in the long term. Leaders are currently ironing out their short-term priorities with generative AI, which will bring about several trends and challenges in 2024, including:
Leaders will need to weigh costs and operational considerations.
Before anything material can happen with generative AI at their companies, leaders will need to decide: Buy or build? Large or small model? Open source or proprietary?
Some will stick with large models. Others will likely opt to invest in smaller models, fine-tuned on internal data. Some will find they do need the large language models (LLMs) trained on billions of parameters but still want to fine-tune those models with their data to ensure they are getting the most out of their investment. Some companies will opt for both, and some will take a wait-and-see approach, watching others from the sidelines to see what is most successful.
On the vendor side, an important, still-debated question revolves around pricing. There’s no standard or baseline for pricing AI features, and some vendors are looking to tack on sky-high per-user per-month pricing. As some vendors pass rising GPU and research and development costs on to their customers, CIOs are still being tasked with cutting spend and will be forced to reckon with ancillary charges alongside the main product they’re accustomed to.
To address this concern, more CIOs may opt to build their own models. The market is so nascent that purpose-built models for specific functions or industries may even not be available yet, and security and data protection are key concerns that persuade companies to build or fine-tune their models at least in the short term.
Companies will face data quality, model reliability, accessibility and governance bottlenecks.
Many companies are experimenting with LLMs, but few of those solutions have gone into production. Leaders want to bring data to the masses but haven’t quite figured out how yet. Many software companies—including my company, Databricks and Microsoft, Glean, Replit and GitHub, among others—are enhancing their products by implementing generative AI capabilities. We are also seeing an increasing number of other vertical industries implementing generative AI offerings tailored to their industry use cases.
A core bottleneck to “doing generative AI” revolves around applying the technology in a safe, effective and reliable manner. Leaders are grappling with data issues, specifically access to, and governance of, an organization’s corpus of data.
In a Workday survey of more than 2,300 executives globally, for example, just 4% of respondents described their data as fully accessible—demonstrating a massive gap between what many companies want to do with generative AI and what they’re actually equipped to do.
The accuracy and reliability of what is generated by LLMs is also an important research and industry challenge worth addressing. Departments that require a high degree of accuracy—for example, legal, finance and compliance—will adopt generative AI tools more slowly than other functions, but will still see benefits. However, models must be more reliable to bring these teams true value—consider the degree of accuracy needed for a nontechnical attorney or financial analyst to do their work well with the aid of generative AI.
While prompt engineering, retrieval automated generation (RAG) models and fine-tuning can reduce hallucinations, they don’t eliminate them—so I expect more innovation will materialize to address this core concern.
In the coming year, data leaders will be laser-focused on overcoming these foundational challenges. We’ll likely see more companies consolidating their data tools and doubling down on efforts to improve data quality and controls. A recent MIT Tech Review study produced in partnership with Databricks showed that nearly three-quarters of senior technology executives have adopted a Lakehouse architecture, and many others plan to do so.
Where We Go From Here
The work—some experimental, and some successful—teams are doing right now will inform where companies are going to get the most immediate value from generative AI and, subsequently, where they will invest the most money and time. But none of this will be possible in the near term without a newfound focus on data integrity, quality and governance.
Millions of knowledge workers—both technical and business users—will be using various forms of AI-powered assistants in 2024 and beyond. The sheer number of people using these tools gives the technology industry a large sample size to glean insights about how, and to what extent, AI can successfully aid different functions. This will ultimately help inform future approaches, factors for success, and use cases for generative AI.
Like all great technologies, generative AI will evolve (and even stumble) before it reaches its full potential. We still have a long way to go with generative AI, from boosting its efficiency and accuracy to reconciling necessary regulations with innovation. One thing is for certain: The coming year will be integral in defining what the AI-driven future looks like and how it will ultimately change the way organizations operate.

title: The AI Factor In Political Campaigns: Revolutionizing Modern Politics
text:
In the ever-evolving landscape of political campaigns, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a game-changing tool. By harnessing AI's capabilities, political parties and candidates can analyze vast amounts of data, tailor messages, predict voter behavior, and optimize campaign strategies. As a result, political campaigns are moving towards precision campaigning with messaging targeted at each individual… transforming how politicians connect with voters. So, yes, politicians are trying to talk (or spinning) to you as a distinct person.
AI in Voter Targeting and Campaign Messaging
Political campaigns are leveraging AI for sophisticated voter targeting and personalized messaging. In the 2016 U.S. presidential election, the Trump campaign used Cambridge Analytica's data analysis to target voters with tailored messages. AI algorithms analyzed data from various sources to identify voter preferences and susceptibilities, allowing the campaign to deliver customized messages through social media and other platforms. Similarly, during the 2020 U.S. presidential elections, the Biden campaign used AI to optimize ad placements, targeting voters in crucial swing states with personalized messages. The AI tools analyzed past voting patterns, demographic data, and online behavior to predict voter preferences and tailor messages accordingly.
AI in Social Media and Online Campaigns
AI plays a significant role in managing social media and online campaigns. Tools like Hootsuite and Buffer use AI algorithms to determine the best times to post content for maximum engagement. AI also helps in monitoring social media sentiment, allowing campaigns to gauge public reaction to their policies and adjust strategies accordingly. During Canada's 2019 federal elections, several political parties employed AI tools to monitor social media trends and sentiment, tailoring their online content and responses to align with public opinion.
AI in Fundraising and Donor Engagement
AI is revolutionizing political fundraising by identifying potential donors and optimizing fundraising strategies. For example, the Democratic National Committee in the U.S. has used AI to analyze donor data, identifying patterns and predicting which supporters are most likely to contribute. This targeted approach leads to more efficient and successful fundraising efforts. Additionally, AI chatbots are being used for donor engagement, providing instant responses to queries and facilitating the donation process. These chatbots personalize interactions, making donors feel more connected to the campaign.
AI in Polling and Voter Analysis
AI has transformed traditional polling methods. These AI polling tools offer more accurate and real-time insights into voter opinions. YouGo, an international research data and analytics group, employs AI algorithms to analyze online conversations and conduct surveys, providing detailed insights into public opinion. Moreover, AI tools are used for predictive analytics in elections. They analyze various data points, including demographic information and past voting patterns, to predict election outcomes. This information helps campaigns focus their resources effectively.
Potential Future Applications of AI in Political Campaigns
Looking forward, AI is set to further revolutionize political campaigning. To being with, deep Learning for speech analysis will be used to analyze speeches and debates, providing insights into which topics resonate with voters and advising on communication strategies. Next, AI-Driven Policy Development will assist in policy development by analyzing large datasets to predict the potential impact of proposed policies, helping candidates formulate data-backed stances on various issues. Then, there are virtual AI Campaign Assistants. Future campaigns could use AI-driven virtual assistants to interact with voters, answer questions, and provide information about a candidate’s policies, making campaigns more accessible. In complement, in the unfortunate age of fake news, campaigns will turn to AI for combatting misinformation. AI tools could be developed to identify and flag misinformation in real-time, ensuring that voters have accurate information about candidates and issues. Finally, politicians will engage AI for enhanced security measures. AI could be instrumental in enhancing the cybersecurity of political campaigns, protecting sensitive data from breaches.
In the end, AI's integration into political campaigns represents a profound shift in how elections are contested and won. From voter targeting to fundraising and policy analysis, AI's applications in politics are vast and varied. As AI technology continues to advance, it promises to open even more innovative avenues for political campaigning, though this also brings challenges in terms of ethical use and data privacy. The future of political campaigns, powered by AI, will likely be more data-driven, efficient, and tailored to the evolving dynamics of voter behavior and preferences.

title: Are fingerprints unique? Not really, AI-based study says | CNN
text:
Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.
“Do you think that every fingerprint is actually unique?”
It’s a question that a professor asked Gabe Guo during a casual chat while he was stuck at home during the Covid-19 lockdowns, waiting to start his freshman year at Columbia University. “Little did I know that conversation would set the stage for the focus of my life for the next three years,” Guo said.
Guo, now an undergraduate senior in Columbia’s department of computer science, led a team that did a study on the subject, with the professor, Wenyao Xu of the University of Buffalo, as one of his coauthors. Published this week in the journal Science Advances, the paper seemingly upends a long-accepted truth about fingerprints: They are not, Guo and his colleagues argue, all unique.
In fact, journals rejected the work multiple times before the team appealed and eventually got it accepted at Science Advances. “There was a lot of pushback from the forensics community initially,” recalled Guo, who had no background in forensics before the study.
“For the first iteration or two of our paper, they said it’s a well-known fact that no two fingerprints are alike. I guess that really helped to improve our study, because we just kept putting more data into it, (increasing accuracy) until eventually the evidence was incontrovertible,” he said.
A new look at old prints
To get to its surprising results, the team employed an artificial intelligence model called a deep contrastive network, which is commonly used for tasks such as facial recognition. The researchers added their own twist to it and then fed it a US government database of 60,000 fingerprints in pairs that sometimes belonged to the same person (but from different fingers) and sometimes belonged to different people.
As it worked, the AI-based system found that fingerprints from different fingers of the same person shared strong similarities and was therefore able to tell when the fingerprints belonged to the same individual and when they didn’t, with an accuracy for a single pair peaking at 77% — seemingly disproving that each fingerprint is “unique.”
“We found a rigorous explanation for why this is the case: the angles and curvatures at the center of the fingerprint,” Guo said.
For hundreds of years of forensic analysis, he added, people have been looking at different features called “minutiae,” the branchings and endpoints in fingerprint ridges that are used as the traditional markers for fingerprint identification. “They are great for fingerprint matching, but not reliable for finding correlations among fingerprints from the same person,” Guo said. “And that’s the insight we had.”
The authors said they are aware of potential biases in the data. Although they believe the AI system operates in much the same way across genders and races, for the system to be usable in actual forensics, more careful validation is required through the analysis of a larger and broader database of fingerprints, according to the study.
However, Guo said he’s confident that the discovery can improve criminal investigations.:
“The most immediate application is it can help generate new leads for cold cases, where the fingerprints left at the crime scene are from different fingers than those on file,” he said. “But on the flip side, this won’t just help catch more criminals. This will also actually help innocent people who might not have to be unnecessarily investigated anymore. And I think that’s a win for society.”
‘A tempest in a teacup’?
Using deep learning techniques on fingerprint images is an interesting topic, according to Christophe Champod, a professor of forensic science at the School of Criminal Justice of the University of Lausanne in Switzerland. However, Champod, who wasn’t involved in the study, said he doesn’t believe the work has uncovered anything new.
“Their argument that these shapes are somewhat correlated between fingers has been known from the early start of fingerprinting, when it was done manually, and it has been documented for years,” he said. “I think they have oversold their paper, by lack of knowledge, in my view. I’m happy that they have rediscovered something known, but essentially, it’s a tempest in a teacup.”
In response, Guo said that nobody had ever systematically quantified or used the similarities between fingerprints from different fingers of the same person to the degree that the new study has.
“We are the first to explicitly point out that the similarity is due to the ridge orientation at the center of the fingerprint,” Guo said. “Furthermore, we are the first to attempt to match fingerprints from different fingers of the same person, at least with an automated system.”
Simon Cole, a professor in the department of criminology, law and society at the University of California, Irvine, agreed that the paper is interesting but said its practical utility is overstated. Cole was also not involved in the study.
“We were not ‘wrong’ about fingerprints,” he said of forensic experts. “The unproven but intuitively true claim that no two fingerprints are ‘exactly alike’ is not rebutted by finding that fingerprints are similar. Fingerprints from different people, as well as from the same person have always been known to be similar.”
The paper said the system could be useful in crime scenes in which the fingerprints found are from different fingers than those in the police record, but Cole said that this can only occur in rare cases, because when prints are taken, all 10 fingers and often palms are routinely recorded. “It’s not clear to me when they think law enforcement will have only some, but not all, of an individual’s fingerprints on record,” he said.
The team behind the study says it’s confident in the results and has open-sourced the AI code for others to check, a decision both Champod and Cole praised. But Guo said the importance of the study goes beyond fingerprints.
“This isn’t just about forensics, it’s about AI. Humans have been looking at fingerprints since we existed, but nobody ever noticed this similarity until we had our AI analyze it. That just speaks to the power of AI to automatically recognize and extract relevant features,” he said.
“I think this study is just the first domino in a huge sequence of these things. We’re going to see people using AI to discover things that were literally hiding in plain sight, right in front of our eyes, like our fingers.”

PC makers bet on AI to rekindle sales
PC and chipmakers including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Intel are betting that the so-called "neural processing units" (NPUs) now found in the latest chip designs will encourage consumers to once again pay for higher-end laptops. Adding additional AI capabilities could help take market share from Apple.
LAS VEGAS: PC and microchip companies struggling to get consumers to replace pandemic-era laptops offered a new feature to crowds this week at CES: artificial intelligence (AI).
PC and chipmakers including Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Intel are betting that the so-called "neural processing units" (NPUs) now found in the latest chip designs will encourage consumers to once again pay for higher-end laptops. Adding additional AI capabilities could help take market share from Apple.
"The conversations I'm having with customers are about 'how do I get my PC ready for what I think is coming in AI and going to be able to deliver,'" said Sam Burd, Dell Technologies' president of its PC business.
Chipmakers built the NPU blocks because they can achieve a high level of performance for AI functions with relatively modest power needs. Today there are few applications that might take full advantage of the new capabilities, but more are coming, said David McAfee, corporate vice president and general manager of the client channel business at AMD.
Among the few applications that can take advantage of such chips is the creative suite of software produced by Adobe.
Intel hosted an "open house" where a handful of PC vendors showed off their latest laptops with demos designed to put the new capabilities on display. Machines from the likes of Dell and Lenovo were arrayed inside one of the cavernous ballrooms at the Venetian Convention Center on Las Vegas Boulevard.
A Dell laptop at the open house included an AI key, the first button Microsoft has added to a Windows keyboard in decades. The "Copilot" key activates Microsoft's generative AI software that can help with applications and answer complicated questions.
At the moment, the new button summons a cloud-based Copilot, which takes a noticeable amount of time to perform tasks.
"If I put those engines on the PC, I can be faster, lower latency, and I can do more with those engines," Burd said.
To move Copilot onto the PC will require considerably more powerful machines than currently exist - even with the advanced AI chips. For the moment, the new chips are included with more expensive laptops on offer by the PC builders that work with Intel and AMD.
"In the short term we'll be focused more on premium PCs," said McAfee, adding that PCs with advanced AI chips will likely cost between $800 to $1,200.

text:

2024 is not the year of the AI gadget
"We're still trying to get it all to work," said Jay Goldberg, chief executive of D2D Advisory. "You need the silicon and the software, and it's only been a year since ChatGPT launched - people are still getting on board."
By Max A. Cherney
LAS VEGAS: Generative AI fever was expected to sweep through tech land and dominate CES, the year's premiere consumer electronics trade show in Las Vegas this week.
Expect to wait another year, industry observers said.
One company aimed to use AI to disrupt the red-hot meat-grilling industry. Another aspired to play with your pet. A prototype boxing glove that uses machine learning to turn people into better fighters also made its debut. Few of these gadgets captured the wild energy that generative AI did in the 2023 hype cycle.
Just a year after ChatGPT's launch in 2022, companies did not have enough time to translate the excitement of large language models into gadget form.
"We're still trying to get it all to work," said Jay Goldberg, chief executive of D2D Advisory. "You need the silicon and the software, and it's only been a year since ChatGPT launched - people are still getting on board."
The lackluster showing was an inauspicious beginning to a year when investors are expected to look for signs of financial returns from the billions of dollars of investments committed to the heavily hyped generative AI sector.
But profits are not assured, especially in the nascent device sector. On the first day of the trade show, AI gadget startup Humane announced it laid off 10 employees, ahead of the March launch date of its $699 AI-powered gadget intended to replace the smartphone, citing the need to restructure.
One sector that leaned into the frenzy was the automobile industry. Volkswagen presented vehicles with a voice assistant that integrates ChatGPT's technology, that is supposed to let drivers listen to research content on the road. But ChatGPT has a propensity to "hallucinate" erroneous information, and was why Mercedes-Benz launched a virtual assistant that checks some of its answers against data from Google in order to be more accurate.
China-based Mojie demonstrated augmented reality glasses made with plastic lenses that connect to a smartphone. The glasses included an option that lets the user push a button on the frames to activate ChatGPT and display responses to queries in their field of view.
AI startup Rabbit launched a standalone gadget called the R1 that is similar to the voice assists produced by Amazon.com and Alphabet's Google. The device uses what the company describes as a "large action model" to control apps. It sold 10,000 units in a day.
Next year's CES is likely to contain many more gadgets and products that include forms of generative AI after companies have enough time to develop the appropriate hardware and software, according to Accenture analyst Syed Alam.
"I wouldn't be surprised if we see handheld devices that are doing generative AI, and maybe even offline," Alam said.

title: Council Post: Beyond ChatGPT: AI Simulation Is The Next Frontier Of Advanced Computing
text:
Jack Hidary is the CEO of SandboxAQ.
Artificial intelligence is taking a leap forward with new tools that take us well beyond writing essays and summarizing documents. While large language models (LLMs) are adept at text and visual learning models (VLMs) are excellent at producing graphics and short videos, another set of AI tools is needed to address the most pressing challenges of our time: developing medicines for diseases, accelerating the move to renewable energy and storage, creating new materials for automotive and aerospace, developing safer and more efficient water filtration and tackling other key goals.
That’s where AI simulation steps in. AI simulation combines techniques from quantum physics with the power of deep learning to address these challenges.
Let’s first focus on biopharma development. McKinsey published research showing that “the average time for taking a new medication from candidate nomination to launch has been about 12 years.” As for cost, a Deloitte report found that the “average cost of developing a new drug rose by $298 million to $2.3 billion in 2022.” We need cost-efficient and timely drug development that produces safe medicines. The sooner we have them, the faster we can positively impact patients' lives.
Other pressing issues we must solve include bringing new battery chemistry to power EVs and storing renewable energy at scale. We also need a way to remove forever chemicals (PFAS) from water filtration and other key areas of our lives. We have to go beyond just text or image-based AI to crack these larger problems.
The AI Simulation Revolution Has Just Begun
Artificial Intelligence models such as ChatGPT do well when they are trained on large amounts of data. What do we do, though, when there isn’t a lot of data—which is the reality in the majority of cases in the physical world? For instance, if we had lots of data on a new drug for Alzheimer’s disease, we would have already solved the problem. What is needed is a new form of AI that can generate high-quality data based on real-world physics and dynamics. This is where simulation comes into the picture. A simulator is a computer program that contains the key equations that drive molecular or other dynamics and can run the possible combinations and interactions billions of times. Deep learning AI is then applied to this data to optimize for a desired outcome, such as a drug with high binding affinity to a target receptor.
Running billions of simulations of a digital twin of the molecule in a large GPU cluster computer model is far easier, faster and less costly than manipulating a physical experiment in a lab. Along the way, AI models can learn from past simulations to further improve.
Consider ConPLex, a model created by MIT and Tufts University researchers that, according to MIT News, enables them to “screen more than 100 million compounds in a single day.” Simulation is particularly helpful for advancing breakthroughs in challenging, undruggable conditions like cancer or Alzheimer’s, where little data exists for AI to model. In this case, the quantum mechanical interactions between drug compounds and human receptors—simulated on today’s classical computing hardware (GPUs)—create new data from physics and unlock insights that have eluded researchers for decades.
Using simulation, researchers can create drugs that are safer for patients and have a better chance of succeeding at clinical trials by running virtual scenarios of drug interactions within the human body before the first person takes the drug. And they can do it faster and much more cost-effectively by eliminating years of painstaking lab work trying to replicate molecular-level interactions to find the most promising compounds. This ability to impact the physical world is why some GPU manufacturers are doubling down on these new forms of AI.
Other Key Use Cases Of AI And Simulation
The combination of AI and simulation goes beyond medicine. Combining the two technologies helps scientists and others make cutting-edge discoveries in various areas with less time, money and risk than traditional avenues.
Clean energy is another leading use case. While lithium-ion batteries have been integral in powering electric vehicles and helping to store solar and wind energy, they have major limitations. We need batteries that have higher energy density, weigh less and are less expensive to produce. However, performance-testing advanced battery chemistries, materials and designs can take years via traditional methods. Using simulation, researchers can explore countless combinations by using AI to optimize designs and make performance predictions much faster, helping to speed these new batteries to market or optimize them for specific applications.
Other key use cases include materials science, food technology and cosmetics product development. If it’s a tangible item, chances are that AI and simulation can work together to help researchers create a better version of it. For example, using these two technologies, scientists can engineer new types of biodegradable plastics or more sustainable construction materials, minimize harmful additives in the foods we consume, and create skincare and beauty products that do not have some of the toxicities we see today.
Testing In The Real World
AI simulation opens up many new possibilities to tackle large problems. To validate the results of these computer models, we must still put the final suggested molecular structures through real-world testing. There is a continual feedback loop between AI simulation and physical testing that drives progress forward. This is critical not only for safety but also for improving the AI models in use; the more reinforcement learning that researchers program into the development process, the quicker the models will improve.
By strategically using AI and simulation together now, we can make breakthroughs that will create commercial and societal benefits. Key to this success will be the training of engineers and leaders in these novel AI tools. University, corporate and governmental leaders all have roles to play in driving this upskilling. Let’s make sure these powerful tools are democratized across the world so all can benefit from them.
