title: Venture Capital's New Era: AI's Journey From Enhancing Operational Efficiency To Alpha Generation
text:
In the ever-evolving landscape of venture capital, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged not just as a tool but as a transformative force, redefining the parameters of investment strategies and operational efficiency. At the heart of this revolution lies the insightful perspectives of thought leaders like Dr. Mohammad Rasouli, an AI researcher from Stanford University and a consultant in guiding institutional investors through the intricacies of AI for alternative investments with his Bay Area tech company AIx2.
In November 2023, during the Superinvestor conference in Zurich, I had the opportunity to meet with Rasouli. Our conversation unveiled the current and potential impacts of AI on venture capital (VC) funds. From enhancing operational effectiveness to generating unparalleled investment opportunities – commonly referred to as ‘alpha’ – Rasouli explained how leading firms like Sequoia, A16Z, and Tiger Capital are harnessing AI to not only streamline their processes but also to uncover hidden gems in the vast ocean of investment opportunities.
VC’s AI stack: ranging from operational effectiveness to generating alpha
When asked what the optimal AI stack for a VC fund looks like today, Mohammad explained that Sequoia, A16Z, Tiger Capital, Iconiq and others are already using AI tools for two primary goals: operational efficiency and generating alpha. The first set of use cases is focused on anything from data analysis to co-pilot options with the purpose of improving their daily operational efficiency e.g. document generation and process management using generative AI technology, while generating alpha includes more complicated tasks which require predictive AI: from sourcing deals to invest in, matching with optimal LPs that could invest in their fund to recruiting the best candidates to hire for existing portfolio companies. And while finding new potential deals gets the most attention and interest, the opportunities go far beyond that, Rasouli explained. Where a fud should start practically and how to proceed is tailored to its own.
VC firms using AI to disrupt the business: the example of EQT and Motherbrain sourcing nine deals to date
The gold rush for capturing the power of AI is already strated and all mega funds are increasing their investments on data and data science teams. One leading example which is also outspoken about their work is EQT's project Motherbrain, utilising AI to identify promising investment opportunities. Initiated in 2016, it helps EQT Ventures to be data-driven in finding the best tech start-ups. Motherbrain combines external data points, including data in social media, with company data and 140,000 unique EQT historical due diligence to train its machine on finding good deals. Interestingly, Motherbrain platform has grown up to other use cases examples include supporting tracking of company life-cycles and assisting in making faster, more substantiated decisions. EQT has provided the Motherbrain capabilities also to its portfolio companies HR teams, particularly for finding talents to hire. Motherbrain's capabilities include market analysis, expert sourcing, and competitors’ benchmarking which significantly enhances EQT's dealmaking workflow and thematic deal sourcing. Perhaps the most interesting result is that EQT Ventures’ investment thesis was proven with nine investments fully sourced by Motherbrain. These AI sourced investments include Peakon, AnyDesk, CodeSandbox, Griffin, Handshake, WarDucks, Standard Cognition, Netlify and Anyfin. The fund states that all of these companies would not have been identified without Motherbrain.
Platform approach yielding maximum returns
But the applications don’t stop there: a private equity or a later stage investment fund is looking for other opportunities due to the fact that they are sitting on a wealth of historical financial and performance data on a given company and industry segment. As a result, some VCs are using AI to make their startups grow faster, or even transform them to embed AI in the way they make products similar to EQT work described above, while others may give the AI an investment seat in the investment committee e.g. General Atlantic PE - so that the machine can vote just like a human.
Rasouli claims that due to the wide variety of use cases and existing success stories across investment verticals, the VC funds of the future will leverage a so called “Platform Approach” where AI isn’t used in a fragmented fashion for a single task such as reporting or sourcing dealflow, but instead it is woven into the fabric of the company and works as an integral part of it. EQT’s Motherbrain is one example of such growing platforms inside VCs approach. “Rather than using AI here and there in a fragmented way, or buying solutions sporadically, they will start to have the entire backbone of their investment in a platform that can support the fund end to end. All of these use cases across the investment cycle, from fundraising to finding deals, making the management presentation or meeting the team, executing the deal all the way to transformation and exit” Rasouli concluded.
Using AI for sourcing founders instead of companies - and potentially outperforming humans
Looking for signals doesn’t stop at pattern matching for companies, in fact - the main ingredient in VC investing, especially at the early stage, are the startup founders. Rasouli describes that this technique is used among VC funds and gives an example: “If a founder is working at a reputable company, and suddenly their LinkedIn goes blank, like they don't update their LinkedIn or they don't post anything - they are probably in their stealth mode of making a startup. So that's the exact time a VC wants to approach them, make a connection and talk to them about their company and fundraising plans”. In this way they are able to beat the competition by getting in the deal early and finding hidden gems on this competitive market. He also adds that more than 200 academic papers were published on the topic of using AI in VCs just in the last two years. One example includes a whitepaper on Human Versus Computer: Benchmarking Venture Capitalists and Machine Learning Algorithms for Investment Screening where the authors concluded that, after anonymising 10 company one pagers, the algorithm was in fact better than 111 VC professionals at making an investment decision. This isn’t to say humans will get replaced, but as the author advocates, the funds could benefit from an augmented solution where algorithms narrow down the upper part of the deal-flow funnel, allowing VC investment professionals to focus their manual efforts on the lower part of the funnel. As Rasouli concluded: ”They train the machine off of those patterns and then ask the machine the same question. And the machine was actually outperforming the investors. That's the signal - that's one of the ways that they were trained. They showed these algorithms are better than humans in choosing the good investment opportunities when it comes to startups and there are so many algorithms out there! They are actively looking at the profile of a company, the founder, financial history and whatever data exists, and see if it's a good match to the investment thesis of a VC”.
Black box, privacy concerns and failed AI experiments at funds
How do we know why the machines have chosen the startups they did? “The fundamental technology behind all these AI techniques is the neural network. Neural networks are however black boxes, we do not yet know mathematically why they decide for a given option. It's hard to understand what they do. And once you give them a lot of data - that's the whole magic of the neural network. Once fed with proper and substantial data, the magic happens suddenly and this pattern recognition is done better than humans could ever do” Rasouli clarifies.
The other challenge of neural networks is that they tend to record the information about their inputs in their nodes in complicated ways that we do not know. Therefore, they may put the fund at privacy risks if there are sensitive inputs used for training the machine. This is a challente becasea at the same time, we do not yet know how to delete a certain input used for training the neural network from its nodes. This all means the best practical approach for risk-free AI is to avoid passing sensitive information for training neural networks in the first place. This does not mean not using the AI tool at all, rather to take tailored engineering approaches for each fund to mitigate the risk.
Rasouli also confirms that private investments are more complicated than public investments. Why? Because the private VC market requires two sided matching. When you think about it from an engineering perspective, the algorithm is matching a good asset to an appropriate VC fund, with a matching thesis, so it is a “recommendation algorithm” - making the entire process more complex due to additional variables. That's not the case with hedge funds and stock trading as it is simply one sided matching, making it a “search algorithm” which is much simpler process for an AI tool to solve.
Saving senior partners up to 80% of time by automating reporting and investment memos
One of the most important tasks of any fund is reporting back to their LPs. Preparing the standard reporting package of quarterly reports, financial statements, capital account statements tends to be a very tedious and time consuming task - yet a crucial element of the business as these documents are sent back to their LPs. Rasouli explains that this is a perfect example where AI can save time and money: “That use-case is a great example of a low hanging fruit that applies to almost all VCs. This is absolutely something that should be done with machines - and I expect in the next two years no one is going to do it the way they do it today. Now, in my own company AIx2, with my own team, we do have similar use cases. One of the clients we serve managed to save 80% of their senior investment time using such tools. It is a reality that actually writing the investment memos and reporting back to LPs is most of their day to day business - and now they have the extra time and money to focus on their business”. Rasouli further concluded that this kind of use cases are particularly attractive as you don’t need a lot of data to automate such processes. For example, you only need approx. 10 examples of previous reporting and investment memos for the LLM to be able to replicate your structure, format and style.
The Buy vs. Build Dilemma in AI Integration
VC firms face a crucial decision: building an in-house AI system or purchasing existing tools. Larger firms may opt for in-house development due to their resources and specific needs - which Rasouli explains is a sensible and bold move they should be taking. This in-house development aligns closely with their specific operational needs and investment strategies, offering a tailored solution that maximises the advantages of AI in their processes. However, for smaller funds, this approach might be impractical, considering the complexities and costs involved in software development.
An alternative is to use off-the-shelf AI tools, but this approach can lead to a fragmented ecosystem of multiple software solutions that may not integrate well.
The ideal solution for funds lies in a middle ground – partnering with a third party to first develop a tailored AI strategy and then implement the priority use cases in a coherent platform approach that also allows future use cases to be extracted from that. This approach allows VC firms to benefit from specialised AI capabilities without the burden of building and maintaining an extensive internal IT infrastructure. Rasouli explains that the criteria for a good AI development third party partner can be summarised as follows. While drawing on practices similar to those at McKinsey, his alma mater and previous employer, for providing this list, Rasouli also emphasizes that AI transformation requires deep AI engineering capabilities.
- Expertise in AI Technology: The AI development third party partner should not only have skilled engineers and machine learning experts but also data scientists who are deeply knowledgeable about AI. They should be capable of understanding and applying the latest research and developments in the field to ensure that the technology remains cutting-edge and competitive. Research at top academic or industry labs is a signal for such capability.
- Domain Knowledge in Investment: It’s crucial that the AI development partner you choose has a thorough understanding of the investment business and experience working with venture capital firms. This ensures that the AI solutions developed are relevant and customised to meet the specific needs of the VC industry.
- Collaborative Partnership Approach: The AI partner should adapt at working closely with VC firms in a way that minimises friction. This includes understanding the nuances of the investment industry and implementing AI solutions in a manner that is minimally disruptive yet maximally beneficial to the VC firm’s operations. It also requires understanding the fund culture to inform development.
- Comprehensive Strategy Development: A good AI partner should help develop a complete AI strategy that aligns with the overall vision and goals of the VC firm. This strategy should encompass all elements from data pipeline setup and operational changes to risk analysis and cultural transformation within the firm.
- Strategic Implementation: The partner should assist in strategically selecting and prioritising use cases for AI implementation. This involves identifying applications that are most likely to succeed and provide tangible benefits, thereby ensuring a positive initial experience with AI within the firm.
- Educating fund managers with AI: successful AI transformation should be led by fund top managers. To do so, those managers should be empowered with knowledge about AI that is required for their business, and what it takes to successfully implement it in their fund. They should know the magic vs myth of AI. A good AI development partner should be able to offer this critical piece to the fund.
- Capability to advice on AI transformation of portfolio companies: AI transformation of the portfolio companies, in synergy with the fund AI transformation, requires its own strategy approach and steps e.g. how to choose priority portfolio companies, priority use cases for them, and the degree of involvement by the fund for portfolio companies AI transformation (advise only, to catalyse, or implement). A good AI partner should be knowledgeable and capable to develop such a strategy for the fund and guide managers in the process.
In essence, the ideal AI partner combines technical expertise, industry-specific knowledge, a collaborative approach, strategic planning capabilities, and a comprehensive view of how AI can transform a VC firm’s operations.

title: SAP BrandVoice: Why Generative AI Is A Game Changer For Supply Chains
text:
“To me, supply chains of the future will be steered by human creativity but powered by AI and intelligent technologies.”
That is quote comes from Deloitte’s Subit Mathew, who I had the pleasure of talking to in a recent Future of Supply Chain podcast. It was clear from our conversation that generative AI is the logical next step to automate supply chains and empower employees to become far more efficient than they are today with traditional tools.
What Companies Should Ask Themselves Before Deploying Gen AI
AI can be a game changer for supply chains drowning in data. The challenge is to put this data into the business context of the specific job function or job at hand, to help automate mundane, repetitive jobs and empower the worker of tomorrow with the right information, predictions and suggestions.
As Subit explained, “AI is all about doing things that you did before differently. And doing different things that you didn't even know how to do before!”
Subit believes companies need to segment their AI strategies into three different categories:
Improve efficiency to do the things it does today in a different, more accelerated fashion.
Improve the user experience to become more intuitive and provide contextual information.
Deliver new processes and innovation previously not had in the organization.
“A lot of companies are looking at establishing AI Center of Excellence, which really look at it from multiple perspectives,” said Subit.
This involves answering several questions:
- What is the right governance model you want to put in place around what initiatives do you even prioritize?
- How do you prioritize the use cases you want to go after?
- How do you quantify the value of what you want to go after?
- What is the technology fabric that you're going to use to accomplish this?
"This is the value of where an ERP platform such as SAP comes in,” said Subit. “If you combine them with some of the large language models out there, it opens itself up to doing really remarkable things.”
Will AI replace humans?
This is a question that comes up in every discussion about any game changing technology. I heard a great comment recently, “AI will not replace humans, but humans that leverage AI, will replace humans that don’t use AI!”
Subit tends to agree with this summation believing that effective deployment of Gen AI, or AI, in general, is about how to augment the workforce to do things better.
“Can you free up capacity for folks to focus on more value-added activities and let the platform run with everything else?,” he asked.
Generative AI is not unlike technological advances that came before – those who leverage the technology will be poised for success, and new, more value added, jobs will be created. Embracing changes like this can be difficult, but if one wants to remain relevant then embrace change they must.
What does this mean for supply chains?
AI is predicted to take supply chain resiliency to the next level by leveraging the vast amount of data now available across the enterprise.
When AI tools are added into every layer of the supply chain it will yield hyper-predictive and efficient processes that will change the way goods flow from suppliers, through the factories and warehouses to the consumer.
Further, AI will allow users to leverage insights, recommendations, and automation to predict events – making more informed decisions and ultimately modernizing functions across the supply chain.
As an example, having a complete picture of the daily demand is essential to optimize profitability, deliver high customer service levels, and enable accurate supply planning. AI-powered demand sensing algorithms can produce accurate short-term forecasts daily by efficiently parsing high volumes of diverse data which was impossible to achieve with traditional forecasting methods.
ZF Friedrichshafen, a global technology innovator in mobility for the automotive industry, utilizes demand planning capabilities in SAP Integrated Business Planning to quickly anticipate and adapt to shifting demand. By using AI embedded within SAP IBP, ZF Friedrichshafen decreased its forecast turnaround time by 92%, freeing planners from time-consuming, repetitive tasks. As a result, the company now enjoys flexible control over levels of the supply chain, including location, product, channel, and customer.
“Imagine if you can actually take your Integrated Business Platform, put AI on top of it and be able to simulate any and all supply chain events that could happen,” said Subit. “You have a set of answers before it actually even happens.”

title: OpenAI sets rules to combat election misinformation. It’s been tried before | CNN Business
text: As concerns swirl about the disruption artificial intelligence could cause for the 2024 elections, OpenAI on Monday declared that politicians and their campaigns are not allowed to use the company’s AI tools. The restrictions also extend to impersonation. Under its policies, OpenAI said in a blog post, users may not create chatbots posing as political candidates or government agencies and officials, such as the secretaries of state who administer US elections. The announcement shows how OpenAI is attempting to get ahead of criticism that artificial intelligence — which has already been used this election cycle to disseminate fake images — could undermine the democratic process with computer-generated disinformation. OpenAI’s policies echo those implemented by other large tech platforms. But even social media firms that are much bigger than OpenAI, and that dedicate massive teams to election integrity and content moderation, have often shown that they struggle to enforce their own rules. OpenAI is likely to be no different — and a lack of federal regulation is forcing the public to simply take the companies at their word. A patchwork set of policies is slowly emerging among Big Tech platforms when it comes to so-called “deepfakes,” or misleading content created by generative artificial intelligence. Meta said last year it would bar political campaigns from using generative AI tools in their advertising and require politicians to disclose the use of any AI in their ads. And YouTube announced it would require all content creators to disclose if their videos feature “realistic” but manipulated media, including through the use of AI. The varying sets of rules, which cover different types of content creators under different scenarios, underscore that there is no uniform standard governing how artificial intelligence can or should be used in politics. The Federal Election Commission is currently considering whether US regulations against “fraudulently misrepresenting other candidates or political parties” extend to AI-generated content, but it has yet to issue a determination on the matter. In Congress, some lawmakers have proposed a national ban on the deceptive use of AI in all political campaigns, but that legislation has not advanced. In a separate push to create AI guardrails, Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer has said AI in elections is an urgent priority but spent much of last year holding closed-door briefings to bring senators up to speed on the technology in preparation for lawmaking. The lack of clarity surrounding regulation of AI deepfakes has some campaign officials scrambling. President Joe Biden’s reelection campaign, for example, is working to develop a legal playbook for how to respond to fabricated media. “The idea is we would have enough in our quiver that, depending on what the hypothetical situation we’re dealing with is, we can pull out different pieces to deal with different situations,” Arpit Garg, deputy general counsel for the Biden campaign, previously told CNN, adding that the campaign intends to have “templates and draft pleadings at the ready” that it could file in US courts or even with regulators outside the country to combat foreign disinformation actors. Efforts such as the Biden campaign’s highlight how even as tech platforms claim to be prepared for AI’s impact on elections, there is little trust that the companies are fully capable of following through.

title: Council Post: Navigating The Digital Frontier: Key Trends In Business Transformation For 2024
text:
Salvador Ordorica is the CEO of The Spanish Group LLC, a first-class international translation service that translates over 90 languages.
Over the last three years, especially since the emergence of Covid-19, businesses have transformed faster than ever. As a business owner myself, I had to automate many of my processes and make them more suited to a digital landscape. However, even after the world started to go back to normal, these changes stayed in place, and the business world continues to transform each day.
But how do we, as business owners, stay on top of the ever-changing digital solutions? The best way is to inform ourselves of the latest trends and adapt and adjust our company structures so we continue to grow.
As we begin the new year, I have spotted various key trends that I believe will be critical for business growth. Below are my top five digital transformation trends you should follow and implement into your own plan for this year.
Why Digital Business Transformation Is Important
People often tell us to "follow the latest trends" in business transformation, but what’s the real reason behind this? There are actually a few reasons why you should care about updating the digital side of your company based on the current climate:
• We’re living in the digital age where many consumers require modern tools and methods to help make their journey with you easier.
• Digital transformation strategies help you do more in less time, which can enhance your client satisfaction score—resulting in better reviews and more referrals.
• The right digital solutions can encourage team members to collaborate better, streamlining your processes and making them more productive.
Five Key Trends For 2024
1. Embracing AI Technology
AI has been in development for years, but it wasn’t until 2023 that generative AI really made a mainstream appearance. Artificial intelligence technology has shown how beneficial it can be for businesses, but there are also a few problems that have arisen with its implementation as well. However, AI tools are frequently updating their software, meaning it’ll no doubt make a more significant difference in various industries in 2024.
No matter what sector you’re in, there’s likely a form of AI technology that can help benefit your business, for example, for customer support. However, it is crucial to acknowledge that even with its rapid advancements, it can never fully replace the nuanced capabilities of human work and intelligence.
The complexity of human cognition, emotional understanding and creativity remains unmatched by AI systems. Therefore, it is imperative to recognize the symbiotic relationship between AI and human expertise. Knowing when and how to leverage AI effectively becomes paramount in maximizing its potential.
2. Multilayered Cybersecurity
One of the most important aspects of any business is ensuring the privacy of its customers, which is why it’s something that should be put on top of the roster for business transformation in 2024. Too many customers believe that brands are protecting their data and information as they should, so I suggest companies start taking a multilayered approach to cybersecurity.
A multilayered approach involves implementing not just one but various cybersecurity solutions, making it harder for hackers to get hold of sensitive information. Some of these solutions can include implementing robust firewalls, SSL encryption technology, two-factor authentication and regular security audits. You’ll build the trust of your customers and be able to work on other areas of your business with peace of mind.
3. Personalized Content
Content has become much more digital in the last few years, as fewer companies are using flyers and billboards and, instead, moving to social media and other online platforms. One reason for this is because targeting your customer base and tracking your results is easier. However, for the best approach, add a level of personalization to your content to suit the individual interests of the demographics you wish to approach.
Personalizing your content and other digital strategies can give you a much better chance of generating leads and new customers. With more businesses doing it in the next year, I recommend you jump on the boat and ensure you stay on top of the competition.
4. Integrating A Hybrid Working Model
We all expected to see the great return to offices in the last year, but many businesses continued to work remotely or even integrated a hybrid working model in their company’s structure. We will no doubt continue to see more enterprises introduce these models into their workplace in the next year, as they often offer a higher level of equality for employees.
When your company structure is mainly based on working online, you offer opportunities to more people who may never have been able to attend the office before. This doesn’t only help them, but you open up your employee pool to those with a much better skill set, setting you up for future success.
5. More Robust Automation
Complex business structures and processes are a thing of the past, as both employees and customers want simpler, more standardized methods. Every year, more robust automation is a digital business transformation trend, purely because we’re always looking for ways to streamline processes and enhance efficiency within a company.
Automation tools are becoming much more commonplace within businesses, and I have no doubt this will continue into 2024. If you want to get more done efficiently and help your clients get the most out of your products or services, consider integrating relevant automation software to reduce manual errors and keep your company on top.
You can never know for sure what’s going to happen this year, but you can definitely predict the various possibilities. I have given you the top five digital business transformation trends I see that different companies will follow, and I suggest you consider implementing them yourself for better growth and success.

title: Council Post: Unleashing The Power Of Data Analytics In Marketing And Events
text:
Sonali Nair is the Chief Executive Officer at Segment Agency.
They say the only constant in life is change, and the events landscape is no exception. Driven by the relentless advance of technology, the industry is undergoing significant transformation and growth, which can make it hard for event planners to keep up. Did you know that 73% of event marketers reported budget increases in 2023?
As we strive to create unforgettable experiences, one key to continued success is data. And the more the better. According to Statista, around 328.77 million terabytes of data are created each day. But how can you harness it to make a meaningful impact in your marketing and event strategy?
As the CEO of an agency that specializes in event marketing and strategy, I'd like to share some insights on the power of data when planning events and the strategies we've found success in.
The Transformative Impact of Data Analytics in Event Planning
While nothing compares to an actual crystal ball, having the right data at your fingertips can come close! By harnessing the vast amounts of data available, event planners can gain incredibly valuable insights into audience behavior, preferences and dominant trends.
The one-size-fits-all method of event planning is a thing of the past. With data analytics, you can personalize and customize event themes and content, crafting a frictionless experience that resonates with each individual. With the right data at hand, you can dissect attendee preferences, curate custom content, deliver the right message at the right time, create better networking opportunities and enable exceptional experiences, whether virtual, in-person or hybrid.
And it’s worth it. According to braindate, the impact of personalizing your events is significant, including:
• Increased attendee satisfaction.
• Higher event ROI.
• Enhanced brand loyalty.
• Competitive differentiation.
How to Measure Success
We all know that event success is based on far more than just the number of attendees you register. How can you effectively measure the success and ROI of your event?
• Set and track key performance indicators (KPIs). Be sure to set your KPIs well before you start planning. Define specific, measurable KPIs that align with the objectives of your event. These might include attendance numbers, engagement levels and conversion rates. Utilize tools like event management platforms to monitor KPIs in real time.
• Analyze post-event surveys. Design and deliver surveys that touch on attendee satisfaction, relevance of the content delivered and overall experience (you can get as in-depth as you want to here!). Be sure to incorporate both quantitative questions and open-ended questions for qualitative insights on attendee sentiment.
• Monitor social media: Leverage social media-monitoring tools to track mentions, engagement and overall attendee reactions. Analyze conversations online to gauge audience reactions and identify trends and feedback that can help inform future plans.
• Demonstrate ROI: Calculate your ROI by comparing event expenses to generated revenue and use your data to showcase tangible outcomes that align with your KPIs (lead generation, sales conversions, etc.). Provide your stakeholders with a clear picture of the financial impact and value created.
Optimizing Event Attendee Experiences Through Data Analytics
To unlock the full potential of your data, you need a strategic approach. Here are some of the things I regularly consider when event planning:
• Enhance logistics and flow: Look at historical data to identify any potential bottlenecks and optimize the registration process while streamlining event operations for a more efficient flow.
• Incorporate technology for seamless engagement: Integrate interactive elements like audience response systems to get immediate feedback, and implement event apps to enhance attendee participation. Interactive tech and apps allow you to collect valuable data on attendee interactions and preferences.
• Real-time data feedback for customization: Be sure to capture and analyze data on site during your event for immediate insights so you can make adjustments and customize experiences in real time to enhance personalization.
• Utilize insights for continuous improvement: Analyze your data post-event to identify areas of success and improvement, and refine future event planning strategies based on feedback and attendee behavior.
Overcoming Data and Privacy Challenges
Harnessing the power of data comes with responsibility. The landscape of data and privacy rules and regulations continues to evolve and must be taken seriously.
Navigating regional regulations is also a critical aspect of responsible data management. The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in Europe and the Canadian Anti-Spam Legislation (CASL) are two examples of the global shift toward stricter data protection laws, but they certainly aren’t the only ones. As an event planner, it’s your responsibility to stay informed about regulations, tailoring your data practices to comply with specific requirements both in the region you operate in and where the event is being held. This includes things like obtaining explicit consent for data collection, providing clear opt-in and opt-out mechanisms and ensuring secure storage and processing of data. Overcoming data challenges not only safeguards attendee information but also positions you as an organization that treats data privacy seriously and helps you foster trust with your audience.
What the Future Holds: AI and Machine Learning in Events
The term "artificial intelligence" is everywhere these days, and not surprisingly, there’s a way to incorporate AI and machine learning into your event planning, too. Predictive analytics, fueled by AI, allows you to more accurately predict attendee preference and event trends, informing everything from content creation and personalization to logistics and resource allocation. Machine learning can also provide you with real-time insights into attendee preferences, which allows you to adjust schedules or pivot content delivery.
Anticipating future trends can be difficult (who could have predicted the shift in events in 2020 or where AI would take us in 2023?), but having a proactive mindset helps. Continue to explore emerging technologies, consumer behaviors and industry innovations so you can meet current audience expectations but also stay ahead of the curve in the rapidly evolving landscape of event planning.

title: Council Post: How To Prepare Your Data For GenAI
text:
Chief Product Officer at Nasuni.
The recent events at OpenAI were extreme, but we should expect a little chaos as increasingly advanced AI models are deployed in the wild.
There will be more board-level debates and disagreements. Technical leaders will have conflicting visions of how to deploy, and we are already starting to see the external forces gathering strength. There will be more and more pressure from a governance perspective as regulatory groups and independent agencies begin to shape and implement controls.
Yet this chaos will not continue indefinitely. Generative AI (GenAI) services are popping up all over the place. While no one can say with certainty which particular AI tools will emerge as the ideal options for the enterprise, we do know that all of these solutions need data.
So, the question every business leader should be asking is: What can you do now to prepare your data for GenAI? On that front, I recommend implementing three fundamental strategies:
1. Assess.
The first step is to assess the state and spread of your organization’s data. Think of this project as a kind of census. You need to figure out how much data you have, its fundamental qualities and characteristics and even where it lives, from the geographic location to the technical storage systems.
There are plenty of enterprise tools out there to help with these sorts of assessments. They will map out your data types, locations and relevance. You’ll want to figure out how frequently different datasets have been accessed, and whether they are critical to your organization’s current work or completely outdated.
This is not as simple as deleting or cleaning out older data, however, as decades-old folders could contain hugely valuable project data that could spark insights, shape your current work or help refine your strategy. This assessment will also help you understand which datasets have specific residence or sovereignty requirements, which is an important aspect of leveraging AI tools.
2. Consolidate.
What you will likely find out during the assessment is that much of your unstructured file data is probably still anchored to specific locations. These could be offices, data centers, factories, manufacturing plants or creative design centers. The nature of the operations at each location will vary depending on your business, but they all create the same overarching problem.
If your entire corpus of data is distributed across multiple sites and stuck in these silos, your organization will not be able to get the most out of AI. Again, AI services need data, and that data needs to be in one place if they are going to do their best work.
So the next step will be consolidating all this data, likely in the cloud, the only storage medium that offers the effortless scale and cost structure to make global consolidation possible. Yet scale is not the only reason to consolidate in the cloud. The initial AI services from Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud and Microsoft Azure are all cloud-native tools. They run in the cloud, so you want your data to be in the cloud as well.
Consolidating your data in the cloud renders it more usable, from the perspective of the AI solution. You will be able to generate more relevant insights because the tools will analyze all of your data, not just a specific subset at a specific location.
Imagine you are operating a large marketing agency, and one of your creative teams wants to pitch a new campaign for a beverage giant. As part of the ideation phase, they might want to leverage an AI tool to generate a new campaign from past campaigns for similar companies. If the associated files from all offices around the world are consolidated in one cloud volume, then one of your creatives could quickly find inspiration from previous work. Otherwise, those ideas might as well be locked away in a forgotten file cabinet.
3. Secure.
The process of assessing and consolidating your data is a perfect opportunity to strengthen and tighten data security. One of the basic tenets of data security is that you cannot rely on people to do the right thing. In the age of ransomware, enterprises must rely on built-in security, and this is your chance to switch to such a solution if you have not done so already.
You want to make sure you have controls around your datasets and who can leverage them. The people using AI services must have the right and the authority to see and leverage that data in the first place. Role-based access control is certainly not a new priority in the enterprise data security world, but it is especially important in the age of GenAI. You do not want anyone leaking sensitive data into a large language model, whether they are doing so maliciously or inadvertently.
During the assessment phase, you will need to map out whether there are compliance exceptions as well, so that when you apply your security rules, you know if certain datasets have sensitive information. If you feed an AI service a collection of files that contain social security or credit card numbers, then you will be liable if anything were to be generated using that data. Your organization is still the steward of that data and it would be your fault for not having the right built-in security tools and controls in place to identify and protect that sensitive information.
Conclusion
These three steps are a good framework for preparing your enterprise in the months ahead. There is a great deal more to do, but the current chaos and AI madness will be sorted out. The technology is too powerful, the demand too great. These tools will be transformative for the enterprise, but if you hope to leverage them effectively, you must take the necessary steps to prepare your data today.
